The sacred relationship between the dreamer's body and the cathedral finds its immediate complement in the profane preoccupations of his waking life. The passage that I was listening to now spoke of the Utensian Polyglot, the third edition of which was used by Martin Luther in his German translation of the Bible. This edition was used for people who could not understand Latin. The first and second edition texts did not include the passage (1 John 5:7–8) that has become known as the Comma Johanneum.

The passage goes on to describe a scene in which an individual is describing the place where happy souls reside. They live in groves, lie on mossy beds, and are near crystal streams that murmur through meadows. The individual then offers to lead the speaker to the end of their journey.

The passage also touches on the relationship between Vellaisamy and Gayatri, stating that the relationship is pure and that the judge can judge this based on their expressions. The judge says that he trusts the relationship between Vellaisamy and Gayatri.

The passage also mentions that in the game Final Fantasy XIV, there are quests that are repeatable, either "daily" quests that can be done each day, or "Levequests," which consume "leve allowances" that the player slowly accrues over time. Dungeons often require multiple players to form a party to enter, but the Duty Support system enables the player to enter alone.

The passage ends with a quote from "The Method of True Theology" by Martin Luther, "he who despises himself and repents of his sin, will find clement God, who is far more merciful to sinners than any father to his son."
